2-5.title: Big Feelings Are Okay!
2-5.description: Learn about feelings and how to feel better!
2-5.script: Hi friend! Sometimes we feel happy! Sometimes we feel sad! Let's talk about feelings!

teachingMoments.content: Show happy face, sad face, mad face - make the expressions together

en.welcome: Hi friend! Do you feel happy sometimes? Do you feel sad sometimes? Me too! Everyone has feelings! Let's learn about them!
en.mainContent: Feelings are how we feel inside. Sometimes we feel happy! Like when we play! Sometimes we feel sad. Like when a friend goes home. Sometimes we feel mad! Like when something doesn't work! Sometimes we feel scared. Like of loud noises. All these feelings are okay! Everyone has them! When you have big feelings, you can do special things to feel better. You can take deep breaths - in through your nose, out through your mouth. You can hug someone you love. You can tell someone how you feel. You can count to five. Big feelings come and then they go. Like clouds in the sky! They don't stay forever!
keyPoints: Everyone has many different feelings
Happy, sad, mad, scared - all feelings are okay
Big feelings come and then go away
Deep breaths and hugs can help you feel better
interactionPrompts: Can you show me a happy face?
What makes you feel happy?
Can we take deep breaths together?
Who do you hug when you feel sad?
en.wisdomMoment: All feelings are okay. Talking about feelings helps!
en.title: Emotional Regulation - Understanding and Managing Feelings

en.welcome: Hey! You know that feeling when you're so excited you can't sit still? Or so frustrated you want to scream? Those are emotions - and learning to manage them is like having a superpower!
en.mainContent: Emotional regulation means understanding your feelings and managing them in healthy ways. It's totally normal to feel all kinds of emotions - happiness, sadness, anger, fear, excitement, frustration, jealousy, pride. None of these feelings are bad! They're information about what's happening inside you. Here's how it works: something happens (a trigger), your brain interprets it, and you feel an emotion. For example: your friend doesn't pick you for their team (trigger), your brain thinks 'that's unfair!' (interpretation), and you feel angry or hurt (emotion). The key is what you do with that emotion. Healthy regulation means: 1) Recognize and name the emotion ('I'm feeling angry right now'), 2) Understand why you're feeling it ('Because I wanted to be picked'), 3) Choose a healthy response (talk to your friend calmly instead of yelling). Some helpful strategies: Deep breathing activates your calm-down system. Counting to ten gives your thinking brain time to catch up. Physical activity burns off stress energy. Talking to someone you trust helps you process feelings. Writing or drawing expresses emotions safely. Taking a break from the situation gives you space. Everyone gets overwhelmed sometimes - even adults! The difference is learning skills to manage big emotions so they don't manage you. It's like training a muscle - the more you practice, the easier it gets.
keyPoints: All emotions are normal and give us important information
Emotional regulation means recognizing, understanding, and managing feelings
Trigger → interpretation → emotion → response
Healthy responses: deep breathing, counting, physical activity, talking, taking breaks
Practice makes emotional regulation easier over time
It's okay to need help managing big emotions
interactionPrompts: What emotion do you feel most often?
Can you think of a time you managed a big feeling well?
What helps you calm down when you're upset?
Who is someone you can talk to about feelings?
en.wisdomMoment: You can't always control what you feel, but you can control what you do with those feelings. That's true power!

6-12.title: Emotional Regulation - Managing Your Feelings
6-12.description: Learn to recognize and manage your emotions!
6-12.script: Hey! You know that feeling when you're so excited you can't sit still? Or so frustrated you want to scream? Those are emotions - and learning to manage them is like having a superpower!

en.welcome: What's up? So teen emotions can feel really intense, right? Like everything is amplified. There's actually neuroscience behind that - and understanding it helps you manage it.
en.mainContent: Your teenage brain is literally under construction, particularly the prefrontal cortex - the part responsible for emotional regulation, impulse control, and rational decision-making. Meanwhile, the amygdala - your emotional center - is fully developed and hyperactive. This creates a mismatch: intense emotions generated by an adult-level amygdala, managed by a still-developing prefrontal cortex. That's why feelings can be overwhelming during adolescence. Emotional regulation involves several skills: Emotional awareness - accurately identifying what you're feeling. Not just 'bad,' but specifically 'frustrated because I studied but still failed' or 'anxious about how I'm perceived.' Emotional acceptance - recognizing that feelings aren't good or bad, they just are. Trying to suppress emotions actually makes them stronger. Cognitive reappraisal - reinterpreting situations. Instead of 'everyone hates me,' maybe 'my friend is having a bad day and it's not about me.' Healthy expression - finding constructive outlets. Art, music, journaling, sports, talking to trusted people. Problem-solving vs emotion-focused coping - sometimes you can fix the trigger (study harder), sometimes you can only manage the feeling (accept the grade and focus on next time). Common traps: emotional avoidance (pushing feelings down until they explode), rumination (obsessing over negative feelings), catastrophizing (assuming the worst), or numbing through screens/substances. Social media makes regulation harder because you're constantly comparing your insides to everyone else's curated outsides, plus the dopamine cycle creates emotional instability. Building regulation skills now literally shapes your brain development. Neural pathways you strengthen become your default patterns as an adult.
keyPoints: Teen brains have fully developed amygdala but developing prefrontal cortex - explains intense emotions
Emotional regulation skills: awareness, acceptance, reappraisal, healthy expression
Feelings aren't good/bad - they're information requiring healthy responses
Common traps: avoidance, rumination, catastrophizing, numbing
Social media disrupts regulation through constant comparison and dopamine cycles
Skills you build now create neural patterns that last into adulthood
interactionPrompts: What emotions feel hardest for you to manage?
How do you currently cope with overwhelming feelings?
Can you think of a time you reappraised a situation successfully?
What healthy emotional outlets work for you?
en.wisdomMoment: Your emotions don't define you - they're weather patterns passing through. You're the sky that holds them all. Learning to observe feelings without being controlled by them is one of life's most valuable skills.

13-17.title: Emotional Regulation - The Neuroscience of Feelings
13-17.description: Understand your emotions and how to manage them
13-17.script: What's up? So teen emotions can feel really intense, right? Like everything is amplified. There's actually neuroscience behind that - and understanding it helps you manage it.
objectives: Understand teenage brain development and emotions

en.welcome: Today we're exploring emotional regulation - a foundational skill for professional success, relationship health, and mental wellbeing. This isn't about suppressing emotions; it's about developing sophisticated emotional intelligence.
en.mainContent: Emotional regulation refers to the processes by which we influence which emotions we have, when we have them, and how we experience and express them. James Gross's Process Model identifies five key points of intervention: Situation selection (choosing environments that promote desired emotional states), situation modification (adjusting circumstances to alter emotional impact), attentional deployment (directing attention toward or away from emotional triggers), cognitive change (reappraising meaning of situations), and response modulation (managing physiological/behavioral responses). Research shows that cognitive reappraisal and acceptance are more effective long-term strategies than suppression, which paradoxically intensifies emotions and impairs memory/cognition. The brain regions involved include the prefrontal cortex (conscious regulation), anterior cingulate cortex (conflict monitoring), and amygdala (emotional processing). Effective regulation requires interoceptive awareness - the ability to perceive physiological signals of emotional arousal before they escalate. Workplace applications are significant: emotional regulation predicts leadership effectiveness, team collaboration, and career advancement more strongly than IQ. The ability to remain calm under pressure, respond to criticism constructively, and manage interpersonal conflict productively distinguishes high performers. Relationship contexts demand sophisticated regulation: expressing vulnerability appropriately, managing conflict without contempt, recovering from negative interactions, and maintaining emotional availability. The Gottman Institute's research shows that relationship longevity correlates more with emotional management skills than compatibility. Common dysregulation patterns include experiential avoidance (the paradoxical effect where avoiding emotions makes them stronger), alexithymia (difficulty identifying/describing emotions), and emotion-driven impulsivity. Mental health challenges often involve regulation difficulties rather than problematic emotions themselves. Building regulation capacity involves: regular mindfulness practice (strengthening metacognitive awareness), physical exercise (managing stress hormones), adequate sleep (essential for prefrontal cortex function), social connection (co-regulation with trusted others), and professional therapy when needed.
keyPoints: Emotional regulation involves five intervention points: selection, modification, attention, reappraisal, response
Reappraisal and acceptance outperform suppression for long-term wellbeing
Brain regions: prefrontal cortex (regulation), amygdala (emotion), ACC (monitoring)
Regulation predicts professional success and relationship quality more than IQ
Interoceptive awareness allows intervention before emotional escalation
Building capacity: mindfulness, exercise, sleep, social connection, therapy when needed
interactionPrompts: Which emotional regulation strategies do you currently employ?

en.wisdomMoment: Emotional maturity isn't feeling less - it's developing the capacity to feel fully while choosing responses wisely. The goal isn't emotional control but emotional flexibility - experiencing the full range of human feeling while maintaining values-aligned behavior.

en.welcome: After decades of experiencing the full spectrum of human emotion - joy and grief, rage and serenity, fear and courage - I've learned that emotional regulation isn't about control. It's about relationship with yourself.
en.mainContent: At midlife, emotional regulation takes on different dimensions. You've likely experienced profound losses, significant victories, betrayals, reconciliations, and the slow accumulation of both wounds and wisdom. What I've learned is that emotional regulation isn't suppressing feelings - it's befriending them. Young people often fight their emotions, trying to wrestle them into submission. Midlife teaches a different approach: curiosity. When anger arises, instead of pushing it away or acting on it impulsively, I ask: 'What is this anger protecting? What boundary was crossed? What do I value that feels threatened?' Emotions become messengers rather than enemies. I've also learned that emotional patterns established early persist unless consciously changed. If you learned to cope through avoidance, achievement, or people-pleasing, those patterns don't disappear with age - they deepen. Midlife offers opportunity for revision: recognizing outdated emotional strategies and building new ones aligned with who you want to be. The body becomes more obviously connected to emotions. Stress shows up as physical symptoms. Suppressed grief manifests as fatigue. Chronic anxiety affects sleep, digestion, immune function. You can't separate emotional and physical health - they're a unified system. This is actually helpful because physical sensations provide earlier warning signs than conscious thoughts. Relationships at this stage require sophisticated regulation. You're managing your own emotions while co-regulating with partners, children, aging parents, colleagues. The ability to remain emotionally available during others' distress while maintaining your own equilibrium becomes crucial. What would I tell my younger self? Every emotion you avoid grows stronger in the shadows. Every feeling you face with compassion gradually loosens its grip. The goal isn't to achieve some emotionless zen state - it's to expand your capacity to hold the full range of human experience with grace. Emotional regulation at midlife means knowing: this too shall pass. Whether it's joy or sorrow, excitement or dread, all emotional states are temporary. You've lived through enough cycles to trust that difficult feelings won't last forever - and neither will pleasant ones. That perspective itself is regulating.
keyPoints: Midlife emotional regulation is about befriending emotions, not controlling them
Emotions become messengers providing information about values and boundaries
Early coping patterns persist unless consciously revised
Physical and emotional health are inseparable - body signals precede thoughts
Co-regulation with partners, children, parents requires expanded capacity
All emotional states are temporary - lived experience proves this
Regulation expands capacity to hold full range of feelings with grace
interactionPrompts: What emotional patterns from youth persist in your life today?
How has your relationship with difficult emotions evolved?
What physical signals alert you to emotional states?
What would you tell your younger self about managing feelings?
en.wisdomMoment: Emotional regulation isn't achieving calm - it's developing the capacity to be with what is, including discomfort. The storms will come. Your job isn't to stop them but to build a sturdy ship and learn to navigate. After enough storms, you trust your ability to weather whatever comes.

36-60.title: Emotional Regulation - Midlife Wisdom
36-60.script: After decades of experiencing the full spectrum of human emotion - joy and grief, rage and serenity, fear and courage - I've learned that emotional regulation isn't about control. It's about relationship with yourself.
objectives: Trust the temporary nature of all emotional states

en.welcome: In 82 years, I've felt every emotion many times over. Today I want to share what I've learned about living with feelings with wisdom, grace, and peace.
en.mainContent: When you've lived eight decades, you understand something profound about emotions: they're visitors, not permanent residents. Grief comes, sits with you, and eventually leaves. Joy arrives unexpectedly, brightens everything, and departs. Anger flares and fades. Fear whispers warnings. All of them pass through. In my youth, I thought emotional regulation meant being strong - never crying, never showing weakness, keeping everything under control. What a burden that was! How much energy wasted fighting my own feelings. Midlife taught me that emotions aren't enemies. Old age has taught me they're companions on the journey. Here's what I wish I'd known at 20: you don't have to act on every feeling. You can feel angry without speaking in anger. You can feel afraid without being controlled by fear. You can feel grief without drowning in it. There's space between feeling and action - and in that space lies freedom. I've learned that emotions often arrive like weather - sometimes there's no specific cause, just a passing storm system. Trying to analyze why you feel sad on a particular Tuesday can be fruitless. Sometimes you just feel sad, and that's okay. Sit with it. It will pass. I've also learned that the hardest emotions carry gifts if you let them. Grief is love with nowhere to go - it hurts because connection mattered. Anger reveals what you value - it flares when boundaries are violated. Fear shows what you care about protecting. Even difficult emotions contain wisdom if you listen. At 82, I still feel the full range. I cry more easily now - happy tears, sad tears, tears of beauty at a sunset. I feel frustration when my body doesn't cooperate. I feel delight when a great-grandchild hugs me. I feel loss as friends depart this life. I feel gratitude for each morning. The difference is I'm no longer fighting any of it. Emotional regulation in old age means acceptance. All of it - the joy and sorrow, the frustration and peace, the loneliness and connection - is part of being human. The greatest emotional wisdom I can offer: learn to hold it all gently. Don't cling to joy or push away sorrow. Both are holy. Both are temporary. Both are necessary. Your emotional life is the texture of being alive.
keyPoints: Emotions are visitors that pass through, not permanent residents
Space exists between feeling and action - in that space lies freedom
Emotions sometimes arrive like weather, without specific cause - and that's okay
Difficult emotions carry gifts: grief is love, anger reveals values, fear shows care
Emotional regulation in old age means acceptance, not control
The full range of feelings - joy and sorrow both - is the texture of being alive
Hold all emotions gently without clinging or pushing away
interactionPrompts: What emotional wisdom have you gained through your years?
How has your relationship with feelings changed across your lifetime?
What emotions do you feel most deeply now?
What do you want younger generations to understand about emotions?
en.wisdomMoment: After 82 years, here's the truth: you will feel everything. Let yourself. The joy, the sorrow, the anger, the peace - all of it is sacred. All of it is temporary. All of it is what it means to be beautifully, painfully, gloriously human. Don't spend your life fighting your feelings. Spend it living them fully, holding them gently, and trusting that all storms pass and all seasons change.
